newsitem.title: USA: CME cattle to fall on larger supply, E.coli fears.
newsitem.headline: CME cattle to fall on larger supply, E.coli fears.

text.p: Larger than expected cattle supplies and growing concern over E.coli bacteria in hamburger meat should combine to pressure CME live cattle futures on Monday, traders and analysts said.

The USDA in its monthly Cattle-on-Feed report said placements of cattle onto feedlots in July in the seven major states were 118 percent of the year-ago level, while on-feed supplies as of August 1 were at 119 percent of a year ago. Both figures were well above industry expectations.
"We have the potential for increased consumer resistance in buying beef on expanding supplies," said Dale Benson, vice president and senior livestock analyst for Dean Witter.
At the same time, the USDA announced a new recall of 1.2 million lbs of frozen hamburger due to possible E.coli contamination. The meat recall was one of the largest on record.

Traders and analysts said the cattle report by itself would have pressured the market, but growing E.coli fears will surely weigh on live cattle futures Monday. October and December futures could fall at least 0.500 to 0.750 cent per lb.
USDA said Hudson Foods Inc would recall 1.2 million lbs of frozen hamburger patties in addition to the earlier-announced recall of 40,000 lbs.

Press coverage of the E.coli story "will make people very leery about going out and buying hamburger," Benson said. "How do people identify whether the beef came from Hudson Foods or not? They don't, so they don't buy it."

But cattle futures will likely start Monday trading the cattle report. Analysts agreed the high July marketing number, at 109 percent of last year, will lend support to August and October and likely encourage bull spreading, buying October and selling December. The much higher than expected placement and on-feed supply numbers will be the big feature in back months.
"It (report) sure could held dampen some of this enthusiasm that had been built in for the fourth quarter," said Bob Price of Cargill Investor Services.
"The marketing number was very supportive, but the placement number is going to pressure the December enough that it could keep some kind of damper on any rally in the October," Price said.

Expectations of tighter cattle supplies going into next year recently pushed live cattle futures to historic high levels. Back months recorded new contract highs in late July, which apparently prompted the stepped-up placement of cattle onto feedlots. Feedlots had a hedge for their cattle, analysts said.
"The last (U.S. cattle) inventory report showed us that we were in a liquidation phase in this cycle" and futures prices moved higher, Price said.

Feeder cattle supplies had started to decline following liquidation of part of the cow herd going into the first part of 1997. But placements onto feedlots during July remained at steep levels despite a five percent drop in feeders.

Chuck Levitt, senior livestock analyst for Alaron Trading Corp, said, "If indeed we had five percent fewer cattle available to place on feed as of the start of the month, July 1st, to place this kind of number tells me that they were digging and looking for feeder cattle any place they could find them to put on feed."
